nameStory: Java water-dropwort gets its name from its native home in Java and other parts of East Asia, where it naturally grows in wet places. The 'dropwort' part refers to the way water seems to bead up and drop off its smooth, waxy leaves after rain or morning dew.
description: Java water-dropwort is a leafy aquatic plant that looks remarkably like celery, which makes sense since they're in the same plant family. This Asian native has bright green, divided leaves and grows in shallow water or very wet soil, typically reaching 1-2 feet tall. It spreads by creeping stems and forms colonies in marshy areas, with small white flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters typical of the carrot family.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Bright green, deeply divided leaves that look strikingly similar to celery leaves, with a crisp texture and fresh, slightly peppery smell when crushed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers arranged in flat-topped, umbrella-like clusters (umbels) about 2-3 inches across, blooming in summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that spreads by horizontal stems, forming dense mats in shallow water or muddy soil

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hollow, smooth stems that feel crisp and break cleanly when snapped, often with a slight purplish tinge at the base

habitat: In New England, this rare plant is found in shallow freshwater marshes, slow-moving streams, and wet ditches. It prefers muddy or sandy bottoms with gentle water flow and full to partial sun. Look for it in areas that stay consistently moist or flooded.

seasonality.spring: New bright green shoots emerge from creeping underground stems, with fresh celery-like leaves unfurling in shallow water.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size with lush foliage and produce their characteristic white umbrella-shaped flower clusters. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish and flowers give way to small seeds before the plant begins to die back.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only underground stems to survive the cold.

funFact: This plant is actually a popular edible green in Korean cuisine, where it's called 'minari' and is featured prominently in the Oscar-winning movie of the same name - yet it's so rare in New England that it's only been spotted three times!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with wild celery or other water-loving members of the carrot family. The key difference is Java water-dropwort's distinctly celery-like leaf shape and its preference for standing or slow-moving water rather than just moist soil.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its many food-related common names like 'water celery' and 'Chinese celery,' this plant shouldn't be confused with true celery or other edible plants. Some members of the water-dropwort genus can be toxic, so positive identification by experts is essential.
compareHints: Java water-dropwort differs from its relative water parsley by having more distinctly celery-like divided leaves rather than the broader, less-divided leaves of water parsley. Both prefer wet conditions, but Java water-dropwort has a more compact, mat-forming growth habit compared to water parsley's more upright stance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water parsley is the only Oenanthe species reliably documented in New England, making it unique in its genus here.
